title: Ines and the Portrait
premise: Folklorist Ines Dunmore returns to her late grandmother's house in the hollow of Vellmarsh to record the village's 'once-sung' songs, only to discover that every photograph taken there now contains an extra empty chair — and the chair is moving closer to the camera. The chair is a threshold: something her grandmother invited in decades ago, bound by a lullaby sung twice, and Ines's documentation has been feeding it a shape to wear. As the house folds inward and the villagers who once sang for her grandmother arrive to finish what was started, Ines must choose between preserving her family's recorded past and burning it, learning that identity is not what is inherited but what is chosen. She survives until sunrise by giving the thing not her face but a found family's faces — the villagers' voices braided into one song — and the portrait finally shows an empty chair, forever vacant.
about_author: Edmund Eriksen is the pen name of a former archivist who spent years cataloguing oral histories in coastal villages before turning to fiction. He writes horror about the violence of memory and the things families keep on purpose.

chapters.title: The House That Keeps Receipts
chapters.summary: Ines arrives at her grandmother Marisol's shuttered house in Vellmarsh, cataloguing its rooms and boxes of tapes with methodical comfort. POV: Ines. Emotional beat: grief disguised as productivity; she documents everything because naming things keeps them safe.

chapters.title: Songs Sung Once
chapters.summary: Ines interviews old Tam Wicker, who agrees to sing a funeral lament but stops mid-verse, pale, refusing to repeat it. He warns her some songs are doors opened from the far side. POV: Ines. Emotional beat: first unease; the village's silence feels less like superstition than self-protection.

chapters.title: An Extra Chair
chapters.summary: Reviewing photographs of the parlor, Ines finds a plain wooden chair in every image — including photos taken decades apart. It sits slightly nearer the camera in each successive picture. POV: Ines. Emotional beat: rational denial curdling into dread.

chapters.title: Marisol's Ledger
chapters.summary: Ines finds her grandmother's hidden ledger: decades of entries logging the chair's position nightly, ending with a final unfinished line — 'It asked me to sing it back.' POV: Ines, with ledger excerpts. Emotional beat: betrayal; her grandmother knew and stayed anyway.

chapters.title: The Neighbor Who Counts Windows
chapters.summary: Elderly neighbor Bree Halloway reveals the house now has one more window than it should, visible only after dark. She begs Ines to leave before the third night. POV: Ines. Emotional beat: isolation begins; the village closes like a hand.

chapters.title: What Documentation Is For
chapters.summary: Ines records herself explaining the phenomenon as a coping ritual, but playback catches a second breathing under her voice. The chair appears in a photo of the recording session itself. POV: Ines. Emotional beat: her armor — documentation — becomes the haunting's instrument.

chapters.title: The Lullaby Twice
chapters.summary: A tape labeled in Marisol's hand plays a lullaby; unknowingly, Ines hums along, completing the second singing. Every light in the house dies at once, and the chair scrapes audibly across the parlor floor. POV: Ines. Emotional beat: guilt and point of no return — she has answered the invitation.

chapters.title: Bree's Bargain
chapters.summary: Bree confesses she and four others were the children Marisol sang to long ago; the chair came for all of them, and only Bree remains unclaimed. She offers a folk remedy: salt, mirrors, and never looking at the chair directly. POV: Ines. Emotional beat: fragile alliance; found family's first thread.

chapters.title: Night One: The Long Hallway
chapters.summary: The house rearranges itself overnight; the hallway to the front door lengthens impossibly. Ines navigates by tape recorder clicks, refusing to look at the chair waiting at the hall's end. POV: Ines. Emotional beat: endurance; survival as stubbornness.

chapters.title: The Village Refuses Her
chapters.summary: Ines flees to the village pub, but the locals won't let her stay past dark — they've paid this debt for sixty years and won't have it renewed. Tam slips her a page of the original song's missing verse. POV: Ines. Emotional beat: abandonment sharpening into resolve.

chapters.title: Whose Face Is That
chapters.summary: New photographs show the chair occupied by a figure wearing Marisol's silhouette, then Bree's, then — horribly — Ines's own. The entity is assembling an identity from everything she has documented. POV: Ines. Emotional beat: identity horror; the archive is becoming a body.

chapters.title: Marisol's Last Tape
chapters.summary: Ines plays her grandmother's final recording: Marisol explains she sang the lullaby twice deliberately, to trap the thing that had been eating Vellmarsh's dead, binding it to a chair instead of a grave. POV: Marisol (tape) framing Ines. Emotional beat: reframe — inheritance as burden willingly carried.

chapters.title: The Four Who Sang
chapters.summary: Bree gathers the surviving children of Marisol's song — three others thought lost or estranged. Together they reveal the ritual's flaw: the binding holds only while someone sings the song alone. POV: Bree, with Ines observing. Emotional beat: found family assembled from shared damage.

chapters.title: Night Two: The Portrait Room
chapters.summary: The house seals them in; every mirror now reflects the parlor where the chair waits, occupied, patient. The entity speaks in stitched-together voices from Ines's recordings, offering to return Marisol if Ines sits. POV: Ines. Emotional beat: temptation — grief weaponized.

chapters.title: Tam's Verse
chapters.summary: Deciphering Tam's stolen page, Ines learns the missing verse doesn't banish the entity — it names it, and a named thing can be refused. But speaking the name requires everyone it has touched. POV: Ines. Emotional beat: hope with a price; unity as strategy.

chapters.title: The Unraveling House
chapters.summary: As dawn nears, the house begins consuming its own rooms, folding the past inward — Ines walks through reconstructed memories, including a kitchen where young Marisol sings to something hungry. POV: Ines. Emotional beat: compassion for her grandmother; understanding the choice she made.

chapters.title: The Offer
chapters.summary: The entity, wearing Marisol fully now, pleads in her voice: sit in the chair, and mother and daughter are reunited forever. Ines nearly does — the chair is warm. Bree's hand pulls her back at the last instant. POV: Ines. Emotional beat: climax of temptation; love tested against identity.

chapters.title: Five Voices, One Song
chapters.summary: At the threshold of sunrise, Ines, Bree, and the three survivors sing the complete song together — the name spoken in chorus, no single throat to claim. The entity cannot take a shape made of many. POV: ensemble, anchored in Ines. Emotional beat: climax; found family as exorcism.

chapters.title: Sunrise
chapters.summary: The house exhales; walls return to true positions, windows count correctly, and the chair stands empty in ordinary morning light. The photographs show nothing extra — except one last image of Marisol, smiling, finally just a photograph. POV: Ines. Emotional beat: exhausted relief; grief allowed to be ordinary again.

chapters.title: What Ines Keeps
chapters.summary: Ines chooses what to preserve: she burns the tapes of the lullaby but keeps the villagers' other songs, recorded freely, sung twice without harm. Bree asks her to stay through winter. POV: Ines. Emotional beat: curation as healing; inheritance refined into choice.

chapters.title: The Empty Chair
chapters.summary: Weeks later, Ines sets the final photograph — the vacant chair in clean daylight — on the mantel as a warning and a promise. She begins writing a book about Vellmarsh, dedicating it to the five who sang. POV: Ines. Emotional beat: quiet resolution; story as guardianship.

chapters.title: Coda: A Knock at the Door
chapters.summary: On the last night of winter, someone knocks — a traveler whose car broke down, holding an old photograph of Vellmarsh that shows, faintly, a sixth figure among the singers. Ines opens the door anyway, singing under her breath. POV: Ines. Emotional beat: bittersweet open door; vigilance as a form of welcome.
